scenes.visual: Title card 'Who Unlocks the Matter?' fades in over a cut-away field: sky at top, a soybean plant in the middle, roots and soil below. COLOUR MAP, same in both films: nitrogen gas = PALE BLUE paired dots labelled 'nitrogen gas'; ammonium = GREEN dots (only inside the nodule); fixed nitrogen carried up the plant = TEAL dots; plant sugar = GOLD arrow and dots; phosphorus = ORANGE dots; bacteria = small PURPLE rods; fungi = WHITE branching threads; viruses = small RED nearly round particles (never cubes); host-to-pathogen harm = DARK GREY one-way arrow. Locked matter carries a GREY PADLOCK icon that springs open when a microbe acts on it. A tracker bar along the bottom reads 'locked' on the left and 'usable' on the right, with a marker that slides. Labelled blocks and cartoons only, never molecular structures. Every number appears only as on-screen text. Anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'. Cream background, 16:9.

scenes.tts: Every protein in your body needs nitrogen, and so does every strand of DNA. The air around you is mostly nitrogen gas. So why can't a soybean, a deer, or you use a single breath of it?
scenes.visual: PALE BLUE nitrogen gas pairs drift through the sky of the cut-away field. A cartoon soybean, a deer and a teenager stand side by side; each breathes in a few PALE BLUE pairs, which drift straight back out. A big question mark hovers, then shrinks into the top corner and stays.
scenes.narration: Every protein in your body needs nitrogen, and so does every strand of DNA. The air around you is mostly nitrogen gas. So why can't a soybean, a deer, or you use a single breath of it?

scenes.tts: Nitrogen gas is locked for plants and animals. They cannot build with it in that form. Two other stores are locked for many living things. One is a dead leaf on the ground. The other is fiber, which your own body cannot digest.
scenes.visual: A GREY PADLOCK snaps onto the cloud of PALE BLUE pairs in the sky. The camera pans to a brown fallen leaf on the soil; a second padlock snaps onto it. A third panel slides in: a cartoon gut with a tangle of plant fiber, labelled 'fiber'; a third padlock snaps on. The tracker bar appears at the bottom with all three padlock icons sitting at 'locked'.
scenes.narration: Nitrogen gas is locked for plants and animals. They cannot build with it in that form. Two other stores are locked for many living things. One is a dead leaf on the ground. The other is fiber, which your own body cannot digest.

scenes.tts: So who could possibly use nitrogen gas? Make your guess before we look inside a soybean root.
scenes.visual: Zoom from the sky down the soybean stem toward its roots. Small round bumps on the roots glow faintly. Three answer cards slide in: 'plants', 'animals', 'some microbes'. They pulse gently.
scenes.narration: So who could possibly use nitrogen gas? Make your guess before we look inside a soybean root.

scenes.visual: Hold on the roots and the three answer cards. A small 5-second countdown ring empties in the corner.

scenes.tts: Some bacteria can. They live inside small bumps on soybean roots, called nodules. There they turn nitrogen gas into ammonium, a form the plant can use. This is called nitrogen fixation.
scenes.visual: The card 'some microbes' lights up; the others fade. Cut-away of one round nodule packed with PURPLE rods. PALE BLUE pairs enter the nodule from soil air spaces; GREEN ammonium dots pass from the bacteria into the nodule's plant cells, where they turn into TEAL dots labelled 'fixed nitrogen'; the TEAL dots climb the root and stem toward the leaves. Label: 'nitrogen fixation'. The first padlock springs open, and its icon on the tracker slides to 'usable'.
scenes.narration: Some bacteria can. They live inside small bumps on soybean roots, called nodules. There they turn nitrogen gas into ammonium, a form the plant can use. This is called nitrogen fixation.

scenes.tts: The plant pays them back. Sugar made in the leaves by photosynthesis runs down the stem to the nodules. Each partner gets something it needs. A partnership in which both species benefit is called mutualism.
scenes.visual: Sunlight falls on the leaves; a GOLD arrow carrying GOLD dots runs down the stem into the nodule, while TEAL fixed-nitrogen dots keep running up. A two-way arrow badge appears between plant and bacteria, labelled 'mutualism: both benefit'.
scenes.narration: The plant pays them back. Sugar made in the leaves by photosynthesis runs down the stem to the nodules. Each partner gets something it needs. A partnership in which both species benefit is called mutualism.

scenes.tts: Now the soybean dies, and its stem lies on the soil. Bacteria and fungi grow on it. They release enzymes that break its large molecules into smaller ones. Nutrients return to the soil. These microbes are decomposers.
scenes.visual: Time-lapse: the plant wilts and a brown stem lies on the soil. PURPLE rods and WHITE fungal threads spread over it. Small scissor icons labelled 'enzymes' leave the microbes and snip big blocks on the stem into small blocks; small dots drift into the soil. Label: 'decomposers'. The second padlock springs open; its tracker icon slides to 'usable'.
scenes.narration: Now the soybean dies, and its stem lies on the soil. Bacteria and fungi grow on it. They release enzymes that break its large molecules into smaller ones. Nutrients return to the soil. These microbes are decomposers.

scenes.tts: The third store is inside you. Bacteria in your large intestine break fiber down by fermentation, without oxygen. They make small acids your body can absorb for energy.
scenes.visual: The gut panel returns. PURPLE rods in the large intestine chew the tangled fiber into small blocks labelled 'small acids', which pass into the gut wall. A crossed-out oxygen tag reads 'no oxygen needed'. The third padlock springs open; its tracker icon slides to 'usable'.
scenes.narration: The third store is inside you. Bacteria in your large intestine break fiber down by fermentation, without oxygen. They make small acids your body can absorb for energy.

scenes.tts: Three locked stores, three microbes that unlock them. Each time, the microbe takes matter apart, and some of it is handed on to other living things. That is why life depends on microbes.
scenes.visual: Split screen of the three open padlocks: nodule, dead stem, gut. From each, a short arrow carries dots outward: TEAL into the plant, small dots into soil, small acids into the gut wall. All three tracker icons sit at 'usable'. Caption bar: 'unlock, then hand it on'.
scenes.narration: Three locked stores, three microbes that unlock them. Each time, the microbe takes matter apart, and some of it is handed on to other living things. That is why life depends on microbes.

scenes.tts: Now look at a grapevine. A bacterium called Zylella grows in its water-carrying tubes and blocks them. The arrow runs one way, from vine to bacterium. A microbe that causes disease in its host is a pathogen.
scenes.caption: Now look at a grapevine. A bacterium called Xylella grows in its water-carrying tubes and blocks them. The arrow runs one way, from vine to bacterium. A microbe that causes disease in its host is a pathogen.
scenes.visual: A cartoon grapevine with cut-away water tubes. PURPLE rods labelled 'Xylella' crowd a tube until it is blocked; leaves above turn brown at the edges. A DARK GREY one-way arrow runs from the vine to the bacteria, labelled 'pathogen'. No padlock opens; the tracker bar dims.
scenes.narration: Now look at a grapevine. A bacterium called Xylella grows in its water-carrying tubes and blocks them. The arrow runs one way, from vine to bacterium. A microbe that causes disease in its host is a pathogen.

scenes.tts: The host is the living thing a pathogen lives in or on. Here, the pathogen grows inside its host and harms it. The vine gives, and gets nothing useful back.
scenes.visual: The vine is outlined and tagged 'host'. The one-way DARK GREY arrow pulses from vine to bacteria. A small empty return arrow from bacteria to vine is drawn, then crossed out.
scenes.narration: The host is the living thing a pathogen lives in or on. Here, the pathogen grows inside its host and harms it. The vine gives, and gets nothing useful back.

scenes.tts: So is a kind of microbe a helper or a harm? Take ee coli. Most strains live quietly in your large intestine. Other strains carry extra genes that make them harmful. People who swallow enough of them in food or water can get sick.
scenes.caption: So is a kind of microbe a helper or a harm? Take E. coli. Most strains live quietly in your large intestine. Other strains carry extra genes that make them harmful. People who swallow enough of them in food or water can get sick.
scenes.visual: Two panels. Left: PURPLE rods labelled 'E. coli' resting in a cartoon large intestine, tag 'most strains: quiet'. Right: a glass of water with PURPLE rods carrying a small extra block labelled 'extra genes', tag 'harmful strain'; an arrow into a cartoon stomach with a queasy face. A label between the panels: 'which strain, and where it lives'.
scenes.narration: So is a kind of microbe a helper or a harm? Take E. coli. Most strains live quietly in your large intestine. Other strains carry extra genes that make them harmful. People who swallow enough of them in food or water can get sick.

scenes.tts: Here is the pattern. Some microbes unlock matter that others cannot use alone, and hand it on. Life depends on them. Pathogens cause disease in their hosts. Whether a microbe helps, harms or does neither can depend on its strain and where it lives.
scenes.visual: The three open padlocks line up on the left with outward arrows, labelled 'unlock and hand on: life depends on them'. The grapevine sits on the right with its one-way DARK GREY arrow, labelled 'pathogen: disease in its host'. Between them, the E. coli pair from the last scene, labelled 'strain and place can decide'.
scenes.narration: Here is the pattern. Some microbes unlock matter that others cannot use alone, and hand it on. Life depends on them. Pathogens cause disease in their hosts. Whether a microbe helps, harms or does neither can depend on its strain and where it lives.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Take-home line on screen: 'Microbes that unlock matter feed life; pathogens cause disease in their hosts.'
